input:
This report presents the findings of a comprehensive staffing review carried out for the dispatch office, to determine whether the current resourcing arrangements remain appropriate. The office currently employs 15 full-time staff, and over the course of last year overtime accounted for 10% of paid hours, underlining the extent to which the office relies on additional hours to cope with its workload.

This overtime is by no means spread evenly across the year: it is heavily concentrated in two seasonal peaks, when demand on the dispatch function rises sharply. Against this background, one option that has been considered is that of replacing half the overtime with one additional hire. Such a hire would cost $65k per year fully loaded, and a hire, once made, is paid for the full year, whereas the overtime it would displace is concentrated in the two peaks and incurred only when the need arises.

Weighing these factors together, the balance of argument points towards retaining the current arrangement. A permanent hire would commit the office to a full year of cost to address a problem that is seasonal in nature, and outside the peaks the additional capacity would have little work to absorb it. In conclusion, it may be worth considering holding the staffing level as it stands and continuing to meet the seasonal peaks with overtime, with the position to be revisited in the event that the peaks lengthen or the underlying workload grows.
target:
Recommendation: the dispatch office holds its staffing at 15 full-time staff and meets the seasonal peaks with overtime. The office manager owns the decision and reviews it after the next peak season, on the paid-hours record for the year.

The office covers its year-round workload within the paid hours of the present staff. Overtime reached 10% of paid hours last year, and nearly all of it fell in two seasonal peaks. The question the review answers is whether a permanent hire is cheaper than the present arrangement, and the evidence is last year's paid-hours record for the office.

Replacing half the overtime with one additional hire costs $65k per year fully loaded. The hire is paid for the full year; the overtime it would displace is concentrated in the two peaks. Outside the peaks, the added capacity has no work waiting for it, and the office pays for hours it does not use.

The trade is therefore a full-year salary against a load that arrives twice a year. The case for hiring strengthens only if the peaks lengthen or the year-round workload grows, and neither change appears in last year's pattern. While the peaks stay short, overtime is the cheaper instrument, and the staffing level is held.
